newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Minister said held as Taleban ousted from town.
newsitem.headline: Minister said held as Taleban ousted from town.

text.p: Afghan forces drove the Taleban from this northern city on Wednesday after a ferocious 15-hour battle, dealing the Islamic militia one of its worst setbacks since it seized the capital Kabul in September.
The ethnic Uzbek troops, who had staged an ostensibly pro-Taleban mutiny against opposition warlord General Abdul Rashid Dostum last week, turned on their new found allies on Tuesday.

The Pakistan-based Afghan Islamic Press (AIP) reported that opposition forces in Mazar-i-Sharif had arrested Taleban Foreign Minister Mullah Mohammad Ghous and its northern military commander Mullah Abdul Razzaq. Independent confirmation of the report was not immediately available.
Meanwhile witnesses in the northeast said Taleban forces captured the opposition town of Pul-i-Khumri in Baghlan province after crossing the strategic Salang Pass.
The town, lying on the main highway from the capital Kabul to north Afghanistan via Salang, was held by forces of Syed Jafar Naderi, allied to the Dostum-led opposition alliance.
Fierce fighting erupted in Mazar-i-Sharif after a Taleban armoured column entered the Shi'ite Moslem district of Saidabad to disarm the opposition Hezb-i-Wahdat militia.

The Uzbeks, led by General Abdul Malik, attacked the column from the rear and clashes spread quickly, as local fighters blasted away at buildings occupied by the mainly ethnic Pashtun Taleban during their 72-hour stay in Mazar-i-Sharif.
Deafening bursts of machinegun fire ripped through the streets and tank, mortar and rocket explosions shook the city through the night and well into Wednesday morning.
By noon it was clear that the black-turbaned Taleban, whose total number was at least 3,000, had suffered total defeat at the hands of Malik's forces and Hezb-i-Wahdat fighters.
The AIP quoted a Hezb-i-Wahdat spokesman in Pakistan as saying thousands of Taleban fighters had been arrested and several hundred killed in the battle.
Black smoke billowed from several buildings set on fire during the clashes. Residents emerged cautiously to sweep up broken glass and assess the damage.
There was no definite word on casualties, but one hospital alone received 19 dead, mostly fighters, and about 50 wounded.
The blood-stained bodies of two bearded Taleban fighters lay in front of the city's magnificent Hazrat Ali mosque, surrounded by a crowd of curious bystanders.

They were among a group of surrounded Taleban fighters who had made a desperate escape bid in four pick-up trucks. One vehicle was stranded outside the colonnaded Mazar Hotel. The others were halted near the mosque. All the Taleban fighters were killed, wounded or captured, residents said.
There was no firm word on what had led to the swift collapse of the Taleban's alliance with anti-Dostum troops, supposed to be operating with them as a joint security force.
Some reports said the Taleban had demanded that Malik's men give up their heavy guns, others said the Taleban had rejected a demand from Malik that their fighters evacuate the city.
Significantly, the fighting flared soon after a lengthy meeting between Malik and Taleban Foreign Minister Ghous and military commander Razzaq.
Residents were visibly delighted to see the backs of the Taleban, who only arrived on Sunday but wasted little time in trying to impose their strict version of Islam on the city.
Swarming through Mazar-i-Sharif in white-flagged vehicles, they broadcast orders that men should grow beards, women should stay at home and girls should stop going to school.

The Islamic militia, which has not experienced much street fighting in its rapid advance across Afghanistan, had to pay a humiliating price for its heavy-handed behaviour in the north, far from its southern Pashtun heartland.
The strait-laced Taleban were never going to have easy relations with the Uzbek troops, many of whom fought for the former communist government that collpased in April 1992.

The Taleban advance through the Salang Pass has cut the last link between Hezb-i-Wahadat forces in the central province of Bamiyan and those of Ahmad Shah Masood, military commander of the government driven from Kabul last September, entrenched in Panjsher Valley adjoing Baghlan.

Masood, said to be seeking peace talks with the Taleban, contacted Taleban Defence Minister Mullah Obaidullah by satellite telephone on Tuesday night, the state radio in neighbouring Pakistan said on Wednesday.
But it gave no details of the contact, reported after a Taleban spokesman said the militia's supreme leader Mullah Mohammad Omar had authorised Obaidullah to talk to Masood.
